name: Tessa McBride

biography.name: Tessa McBride

background.family: Splits weekdays and weekends between divorced parents; has an older half brother she rarely sees.
background.finances: Both homes are comfortable, though parents disagree about which optional expenses they should share.
background.geography: Fort Worth, Texas, with two households on opposite sides of the city.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking; family gatherings mix differing political views and she dislikes being asked to take a side.
background.school: Public high school with many clubs and an active student council.
background.accessOpportunities: Has reliable internet and rides most weeks; a parent attended college and assumes she will attend too.

timeline.story: Tessa made her stuffed animals sit through announcements about the day's pretend picnic. She liked deciding what came first, while a neighbor preferred drawing invitations. Their games sometimes ended when Tessa insisted on changing the story after everyone had already chosen a role for themselves.

She enjoyed classroom show and tell, especially choosing the first sentence that would make people look up. She tried piano lessons because her brother played, but repeated practice frustrated her. A homemade birthday invitation interested her more for its wording than for the crooked letters and pictures.

When her parents separated, Tessa began keeping separate bags at both homes and frequently forgot something important anyway. She took comfort in planning elaborate weekend visits with a friend. She also started making short pet videos, although most stayed unfinished after she lost interest in editing.

Her class collected books, and Tessa noticed that asking for funny books brought different donations than asking for books generally. She liked trying both messages. She disliked arranging the display and convinced another child to do it, then felt annoyed when that child changed the title without consulting her.

She helped promote a school clothing exchange and wanted separate messages for students and parents. Some classmates thought she was making a simple task too complicated. Her first announcement sounded preachy when read aloud, so she rewrote it after a friend laughed at one sentence she had considered excellent.

Tessa joined a student election campaign because she liked deciding what the candidate should emphasize to different groups. She asked an artistic friend to handle the visuals and then kept requesting revisions too late. The candidate lost. Tessa enjoyed discussing which messages reached people more than discussing the final vote.

She is helping publicize a school event with a smaller team. She interviews classmates about why they might skip it and keeps suggesting changes to the invitation. She still delegates artwork. This time she agreed to an earlier deadline, but managing the two household calendars has already caused one missed meeting.

enjoys: Thinking about who will read an announcement
demonstratedSkills: Asking why people might decline an invitation
unfamiliarActivities: Tracking whether messages change behavior over time
motivations: Understanding why one approach works better

biography.selfDescription: I know when something sounds like an announcement nobody will read. I am less good at agreeing that it is finished.
openQuestions: How will she respond when a simple message succeeds without her preferred changes?
Can she give collaborators enough time and ownership?

response.branchReason: Her strongest repeated choice is planning messages for audiences and asking why invitations fail. Business branch customer evidence fits this interest; artwork delegation does not imply dislike of all creation. Management beyond small publicity teams remains untested.
response.financialAssumptions: A summer away and freedom to finish chosen work suggest a rented personal space and a trip. Dining, clothing, and entertainment choices are tentative moderate hopes; comfortable parents do not justify premium consumption or a graduate route.

responseRationales.evidence: She repeatedly delegates display construction and art rather than choosing physical making. There is no direct aversion to construction or repair tasks, so cabinets, tile, appliances, electronics, locks, and machines remain unsure.

She wants to understand why different messages reach people, a transferable interest in comparing explanations, but there is no expressed preference for medicines, samples, organisms, pollution, planets, weather, or fire work. These specific tasks remain unsure.

She likes audience wording and opening sentences, supporting tentative liking for longer written pieces and scripts. She explicitly avoids artwork and video editing, supporting dislike of drawing, set painting, and editing; special effects are untested.

Repetitive piano practice frustrated her and did not sustain her interest, supporting mild dislike of playing an instrument. There is insufficient evidence on composing, dancing, or singing to rate those beyond unsure.

Helping publicize a clothing exchange, book collection, and school event supports liking purposeful volunteering. She has not chosen teaching, therapy, child care, or other guidance activities; these remain unsure.

She enjoys setting campaign direction, adjusting messages, and getting her ideas used, supporting clothing marketing strongly and tentative department leadership and negotiation. Retail selling, financial trading, salon operations, legal representation, and starting a business remain untested.

Her questioning of potential attendees is about audience understanding rather than spreadsheets, networking, calculator operations, delivery, or physical quality testing. These unfamiliar tasks remain unsure.

Missed meetings reflect competing household calendars, not proof she dislikes accurate records. The biography does not show enjoyment or explicit rejection of proofreading, shipping, payroll, inventory, rent records, or mail; these remain unsure.

Everyday essentials cover phone, home supplies, health, and any saved debt or care costs. These are editable estimates, not price quotes. Home and car purchases also take upfront money. Phone, household, and health costs are included; existing debt and care needs are kept. The income range estimates 2026 employee taxes and retirement saving, then adds room to leave 20% of take-home unallocated at the upper end. It is a budget target range, not an income ceiling or a probability.
